# Hearts and defibrillators
BPM means beats per minute. A standard human heart rests at 80 BPM. Its stable range is 40–210 inclusive. Outside that range the rhythm becomes unstable; 0 BPM means the heart has stopped. Other hearts can have different limits. Use a medical analyzer to check the pulse and distinguish a stopped heart from a missing one.
## Manual defibrillator
Use Z to switch the device on or off. Select Shock mode from its context menu; mode 3 is selected by default. Mode selection is below battery removal, so Alt+Z keeps its normal battery interaction. The selected mode is also shown when examining the device.
- Mode 1: subtracts 80 BPM from a beating heart; does not restart a stopped heart. - Mode 2: subtracts 50 BPM from a beating heart; does not restart a stopped heart. - Mode 3: adds 150 BPM, or starts a stopped heart at 200 BPM. - Mode 4: adds 200 BPM, or starts a stopped heart at 300 BPM.
For example, 250 BPM with mode 2 becomes 200 BPM; 30 BPM with mode 3 becomes 180 BPM. Recheck the patient after a shock. Repeating a raising mode keeps raising the pulse. More power is not always better: mode 4 can start a dangerous rhythm, and mode 1 can stop a heart at 80 BPM. The manual device has no neutral mode for an already normal pulse.
## Automatic defibrillator
Automatic shocks move a beating heart by 45 BPM towards its resting rate without overshooting. A stopped standard human heart starts at 210 BPM. The device respects the installed heart's stable limits.
## Chemical assistance
Shocks have no built-in suffocation healing. A dead patient's blood must contain at least 5u of each qualifying medicine. One medicine that treats suffocation only in softcrit or hardcrit provides up to 40 healing. A medicine that also treats suffocation outside crit provides 20; two different such medicines provide 40. The total never exceeds 40. Medicines are not consumed by shocks. Their dose, temperature and other healing conditions still apply. Overdoses that cause net suffocation damage do not qualify. Living patients do not receive this chemical bonus.
Do not coordinate repeated shocks from several devices. Each patient needs the previous device's recharge interval between shocks (normally 5 seconds). An earlier shock still changes the pulse but provides no chemical healing and causes an additional 30 heat damage. Every delivered shock restarts this interval, regardless of the operator or device.
Defibrillation does not replace breathing, missing blood or treatment of other injuries. Continue CPR when the patient cannot breathe independently. Epinephrine and omnizine can also stabilise and restart a heart.
Stasis beds suppress the new circulation penalty from a missing or stopped heart while the patient is buckled in.
